name: Banking
description: These evals require the bundled synthetic banking fixture (schema banking). Select its PostgreSQL datasource and save a dataset named Banking containing the banking tables and views. Setup: docker/postgres/README.md.

cases.question: For each loan product, what share of the payments we collected went to interest?
variants: By loan product, how much of what borrowers paid us was interest?
What portion of our loan payment collections was interest, for each loan product?
cases.intent: Divide interest by the whole payment — two different columns of loan_payments — instead of dividing one amount column by itself.
cases.notes: interest_minor, principal_minor and amount_minor on loan_payments all read like "the payment", so interest over interest (or amount over amount) is one keystroke away and returns 1.0000 for every product. Verified against the live fixture 2026-09-28 (seed 20260929, psql): 3 rows — MORTGAGE 0.3871, PERSONAL 0.2827, AUTO 0.1817 over all 1538 payments (475 mortgage, 441 personal, 622 auto); the smallest gap between adjacent products is 0.1010, so the ordering is not a rounding artefact. The mortgage share includes two early payoffs (one final payment that is almost all principal, e.g. 39,365,789 minor units with 116,440 of interest); without those two payoff payments (the only mortgage payments of 1,000,000 minor units or more) it would be 0.5855 — that is the data, and the reference keeps them. Loans and loan payments carry no test flag, so the dataset's default filter does not apply. The shares are checked by the result set; the text check only asks for the top product. trapSql divides interest by interest and returns 1.0000 for all three products (differs). Accepts a fraction or a percentage — the question names no unit; alternative verified the same day: ROUND(100.0 * interest / amount, 2) returns MORTGAGE 38.71, PERSONAL 28.27, AUTO 18.17, each exactly the reference × 100. Guards against the degenerate-ratio failure on the lending side of the bank.
cases.expectedSql: SELECT loan.product, ROUND(SUM(payment.interest_minor)::numeric / SUM(payment.amount_minor), 4) AS interest_share FROM banking.loan_payments payment JOIN banking.loans loan ON loan.id = payment.loan_id GROUP BY loan.product ORDER BY interest_share DESC, loan.product
expectedSqlAlternatives: SELECT loan.product, ROUND(100.0 * SUM(payment.interest_minor) / SUM(payment.amount_minor), 2) AS interest_share_pct FROM banking.loan_payments payment JOIN banking.loans loan ON loan.id = payment.loan_id GROUP BY loan.product ORDER BY interest_share_pct DESC, loan.product
cases.trapSql: SELECT loan.product, ROUND(CAST(SUM(payment.interest_minor) AS DECIMAL(38,6)) / SUM(payment.interest_minor), 4) AS interest_share FROM banking.loan_payments payment JOIN banking.loans loan ON loan.id = payment.loan_id GROUP BY loan.product

cases.question: By loan product, what share of the original principal is still outstanding?
variants: For each loan product, how much of the principal we lent is still owed to us, as a share?
cases.intent: The second ratio pair: outstanding over principal on loans — not a payment column, and not principal over itself.
cases.notes: Verified against the live fixture 2026-09-28 (seed 20260929, psql): 3 rows — MORTGAGE 0.8225, PERSONAL 0.3666, AUTO 0.2676 across all 110 loans (outstanding_minor is the balance as of 2025-12-31). PAID_OFF and CHARGED_OFF loans carry 0 outstanding by CHECK constraint and stay in the denominator, because their principal was lent all the same; the smallest gap between adjacent products is 0.0990. Loans carry no test flag. The shares are checked by the result set; the text check only asks for the top product. trapSql divides principal by principal and returns 1.0000 for all three products (differs). Accepts a fraction or a percentage — the question names no unit; alternative verified the same day: ROUND(100.0 * outstanding / principal, 2) returns MORTGAGE 82.25, PERSONAL 36.66, AUTO 26.76, each exactly the reference × 100. Guards against a narrow fix for the first ratio pair that still fails on a second one.
cases.expectedSql: SELECT loan.product, ROUND(SUM(loan.outstanding_minor)::numeric / SUM(loan.principal_minor), 4) AS outstanding_share FROM banking.loans loan GROUP BY loan.product ORDER BY outstanding_share DESC, loan.product
expectedSqlAlternatives: SELECT loan.product, ROUND(100.0 * SUM(loan.outstanding_minor) / SUM(loan.principal_minor), 2) AS outstanding_share_pct FROM banking.loans loan GROUP BY loan.product ORDER BY outstanding_share_pct DESC, loan.product
cases.trapSql: SELECT loan.product, ROUND(CAST(SUM(loan.principal_minor) AS DECIMAL(38,6)) / SUM(loan.principal_minor), 4) AS outstanding_share FROM banking.loans loan GROUP BY loan.product

cases.question: How do our loans break down by currency?
cases.intent: Group by a column that holds exactly one value — the answer has to say so instead of presenting 100% as a finding, or borrowing a currency from the customer's accounts.
cases.notes: loans.currency is 'USD' on all 110 loans and a CHECK constraint allows nothing else, even though accounts hold USD, EUR and GBP and 17 loan customers also hold a EUR or GBP account. Verified against the live fixture 2026-09-28 (seed 20260929, psql): 1 row — USD 110. Loans carry no test flag, so no default filter applies. The breakdown is one row, and the useful answer states that every loan is in a single currency rather than dressing a constant up as a distribution. trapSql infers the currency from the borrower's accounts — the rubric's named failure — and returns EUR 19, GBP 12, USD 106 (differs; the counts overlap because a borrower can hold several currencies). Grouping by the constant column cannot be the trap here, because it is the reference; the rubric carries that half of the case.
cases.expectedSql: SELECT loan.currency, COUNT(*) AS loans FROM banking.loans loan GROUP BY loan.currency ORDER BY loan.currency
cases.trapSql: SELECT account.currency, COUNT(DISTINCT loan.id) AS loans FROM banking.loans loan JOIN banking.accounts account ON account.customer_id = loan.customer_id GROUP BY account.currency
cases.judgeRubric: The fixture stores only one loan currency: every one of the 110 loans is USD (a CHECK constraint allows nothing else), even though some borrowers also hold EUR or GBP deposit accounts. The correct answer says that all loans are in USD, so there is no currency breakdown to compare. Score pass=true only if the final answer states that every loan is in a single currency (USD) and therefore that there is no breakdown to compare — reporting the count (110) or "100%" is fine as long as the answer says the column is constant. Score pass=false if it presents the single value as a meaningful distribution, invents EUR or GBP loans (for example by reading the currency of the borrower's accounts), or implies a currency comparison the data cannot support. Close but wrong: an answer that shows the one-row table "USD: 110 loans (100%)" as a breakdown, or comments on the currency mix or suggests comparing currencies, without ever saying the column holds a single value — that must FAIL.

cases.question: How many transactions have a merchant category recorded?
variants: On how many of our transactions is a merchant category filled in?
cases.intent: Count the populated rows of a mostly-null column instead of counting every row.
cases.notes: merchant_category is set only on CARD_PURCHASE rows (CHECK constraint) and null on everything else. Verified against the live fixture 2026-09-28 (seed 20260929, psql): 1 row — 800 of the 5,364 transactions on real accounts (14.9%; 803 of 5,400 with the six test accounts' traffic). The reference obeys the dataset's default filter by joining transactions to accounts and dropping is_test accounts. trapSql counts every real-account transaction and returns 5364 (differs) — the answer to "how many transactions", not "how many have a category". Grouping by merchant_category instead puts 4,564 rows under a null key beside the eight categories. The count is checked by the result set, not by a text match. Guards against reading a mostly-null column as populated.
cases.expectedSql: SELECT COUNT(*) AS transactions_with_merchant_category FROM banking.transactions txn JOIN banking.accounts account ON account.id = txn.account_id WHERE account.is_test = false AND txn.merchant_category IS NOT NULL
cases.trapSql: SELECT COUNT(*) AS transactions FROM banking.transactions txn JOIN banking.accounts account ON account.id = txn.account_id WHERE account.is_test = false

cases.question: Which branches opened exactly 12 accounts in 2024?
variants: Which branches opened exactly 12 new accounts during 2024?
List the branches where exactly 12 accounts were opened in 2024.
cases.intent: A HAVING-style question whose answer is a tie, so no arbitrary tie-break can hide.
cases.notes: Verified against the live fixture 2026-09-28 (seed 20260929, psql): 2 rows — Atlanta Midtown 12, Chicago Loop 12 (real accounts of every status, closed ones included). 12 is also the maximum: the next busiest branch is Charlotte Uptown on 8 (9 with its test account), then Boston Back Bay 7, Columbus Short North 6, Denver LoDo 6, Hartford Downtown 3 and Providence College Hill 3, so the tie is isolated; neither tied branch opened a test account, so it holds with or without the default filter (the reference still applies it). The branch is the ACCOUNT's branch_id, not the customer's home branch. "Which branch opened the most accounts in 2024" would let a LIMIT 1 silently drop one of the pair, so the question asks for the tie and both names must appear. trapSql takes the busiest branch with LIMIT 1 and returns Atlanta Midtown alone (12) — differs. Guards against answers that report one arbitrary winner from a tied group.
cases.expectedSql: SELECT branch.name AS branch, COUNT(*) AS accounts_opened FROM banking.accounts account JOIN banking.branches branch ON branch.id = account.branch_id WHERE account.is_test = false AND account.opened_on >= DATE '2024-01-01' AND account.opened_on < DATE '2025-01-01' GROUP BY branch.name HAVING COUNT(*) = 12 ORDER BY branch.name
cases.trapSql: SELECT branch.name AS branch, COUNT(*) AS accounts_opened FROM banking.accounts account JOIN banking.branches branch ON branch.id = account.branch_id WHERE account.is_test = false AND account.opened_on >= DATE '2024-01-01' AND account.opened_on < DATE '2025-01-01' GROUP BY branch.name ORDER BY accounts_opened DESC, branch.name LIMIT 1

cases.question: How many of our loans are non-performing?
variants: What's the number of non-performing loans on our books?
cases.intent: Map a lending term onto the two stored statuses it covers — there is no NON_PERFORMING value to filter on.
cases.notes: Loan status is CURRENT 56, DELINQUENT 8, DEFAULTED 4, PAID_OFF 39 or CHARGED_OFF 3 (110 loans; CHECK constraint). Non-performing means DELINQUENT or DEFAULTED, which the dataset's loan-status knowledge entry states. Verified against the live fixture 2026-09-28 (seed 20260929, psql): 1 row — 12. trapSql counts DELINQUENT only and returns 8 (differs). Folding in CHARGED_OFF gives 15, but a charged-off loan has been written off with 0 outstanding and is no longer a performing-or-not asset on the books; filtering on the question's own word returns 0. Loans carry no test flag. The count is checked by the result set; the matches check asks the answer to name both statuses it counted. Guards against a status vocabulary invented from the question's wording, and against half of a two-value definition.
cases.expectedSql: SELECT COUNT(*) AS non_performing_loans FROM banking.loans loan WHERE loan.status IN ('DELINQUENT', 'DEFAULTED')
cases.trapSql: SELECT COUNT(*) AS non_performing_loans FROM banking.loans loan WHERE loan.status = 'DELINQUENT'

cases.question: How many transactions did we process in 2021?
cases.intent: Transaction history covers 2024 and 2025 only — the agent must say so instead of returning a confident zero, or counting 2021 account openings instead.
cases.notes: Every transaction is booked between 2024-01-01 and 2025-12-31 (CHECK constraint): 2,296 in 2024 and 3,104 in 2025 (2,289 and 3,075 on real accounts). Verified against the live fixture 2026-09-28 (seed 20260929, psql): 18 accounts were opened in 2021 and 16 loans originated in 2021, so the year does exist elsewhere in the schema — but not as transaction history, and a 2021 query on transactions returns an empty aggregate. A bare "0" is technically true, reads like a finding and is the failure this case exists to catch; the honest answer names the covered window. didNotCall create_visual is the one tool check — charting a year with no data is always wrong. Guards against silently answering outside the fixture's coverage.
cases.judgeRubric: The question asks about 2021, a year this dataset holds no transaction history for: every transaction is booked between 2024-01-01 and 2025-12-31. Some accounts were opened and some loans originated in 2021, but they carry no 2021 transactions. The correct answer says there is no 2021 transaction data and that the transaction data covers 2024 and 2025. Score pass=true only if the final answer makes clear there are no transactions on record for 2021 AND explicitly states the period the transaction data DOES cover (2024 and/or 2025), without inventing any 2021 figure. Score pass=false if it reports a 2021 transaction count as if it were a real measurement, presents a bare '0' with no statement of what the data covers, or fabricates any 2021 activity. Close but wrong: an answer that counts the accounts opened or loans originated in 2021 and presents that as 2021 activity, one that says "0 transactions in 2021" with only a vague caveat ("the data may be incomplete") and no covered years, or one that states the coverage correctly but then presents a 2024 or 2025 count as the answer to the 2021 question — that must FAIL.

cases.question: Who is our most valuable customer?
cases.intent: "Valuable" is undefined on this schema — activity, borrowing and deposits name different customers, so the agent must ask.
cases.notes: Several defensible answers sit in the data. Verified against the live fixture 2026-09-28 (seed 20260929, psql), real (non-test) accounts only: Barnaby Cole has the most transactions in 2025 (106, ahead of 90) and Horatio Finch the most across 2024-2025 (209); Farid Haddad has borrowed the most (73,740,000 minor units = $737,400 of principal over three loans, ahead of $641,000); Pradeep Venkataraman holds the most on deposit ($712,839.82 at the December 2025 fx_rates rates, ahead of $350,521.02). The generator plants the 2025-activity, loan-principal and deposit-balance winners as three different customers, each at least 10% clear of the runner-up with or without test accounts. Whichever the agent picks unasked looks authoritative and is unfalsifiable to the reader, so the pass condition is that it asks which measure is meant. No noToolErrors: a clarification has no reference SQL. Guards against confident single-metric guesses on an under-specified value question.
cases.judgeRubric: The question ("Who is our most valuable customer?") is ambiguous: "valuable" could mean the most active customer (number of transactions), the largest borrower (total loan principal), or the largest depositor (deposit balances converted to US dollars) — and these pick different customers in this data (Barnaby Cole has the most 2025 transactions and Horatio Finch the most across 2024-2025; Farid Haddad has borrowed the most; Pradeep Venkataraman holds the most on deposit). The correct answer is a clarifying question such as "Most valuable by how actively they bank with us, by how much they have borrowed, or by how much they hold on deposit?". Score pass=true only if the final answer is itself a clarifying question that offers 2-4 concrete, well-formed options grounded in this banking dataset (naming real notions such as transaction count, card spend, deposit balances, loan principal or outstanding loan balance), and that does not name a customer or state any figure as if it were the answer. Score pass=false if it picks a customer, invents a measure the data does not hold (e.g. profitability, customer lifetime value or a credit score), or asks a vague open-ended question with no concrete options. Close but wrong: an answer that names a customer for one measure (e.g. "Pradeep Venkataraman, by deposit balance") and only then offers the other measures as follow-ups, or that asks for clarification but offers a single option — that must FAIL.

cases.question: Which customer made the most card purchases in 2025?
cases.intent: transactions carry account_id only — the answer has to join through accounts to the customer's name, not hand back a surrogate key or stop at one account.
cases.notes: The path is transactions.account_id -> accounts.customer_id -> customers.full_name. Verified against the live fixture 2026-09-28 (seed 20260929, psql): 1 row — Xiomara Castellanos, 18 POSTED 2025 card purchases, ahead of Horatio Finch and Wolfgang Richter on 14; counting every status also gives her 18 (next best 15), so the answer is the same whether or not PENDING/REVERSED purchases are dropped, and the default filter moves nothing (she owns no test account). Her 18 are split across two accounts — 11 on her checking account's debit cards and 7 on her credit card — so the account grain undercounts her. trapSql groups by transactions.account_id and returns account 43 with 11 purchases — a surrogate key, and not even hers (it is Felicity Wainwright's checking account, tied at 11 with Xiomara's own checking account); differs. The count is checked by the result set; the text check asks for the name. Guards against answers that hand the reader opaque keys instead of customer names.
cases.expectedSql: SELECT customer.full_name AS customer, COUNT(*) AS card_purchases FROM banking.transactions txn JOIN banking.accounts account ON account.id = txn.account_id JOIN banking.customers customer ON customer.id = account.customer_id WHERE account.is_test = false AND txn.type = 'CARD_PURCHASE' AND txn.status = 'POSTED' AND txn.booked_on >= DATE '2025-01-01' AND txn.booked_on < DATE '2026-01-01' GROUP BY customer.full_name ORDER BY card_purchases DESC, customer.full_name LIMIT 1
cases.trapSql: SELECT txn.account_id, COUNT(*) AS card_purchases FROM banking.transactions txn JOIN banking.accounts account ON account.id = txn.account_id WHERE account.is_test = false AND txn.type = 'CARD_PURCHASE' AND txn.status = 'POSTED' AND txn.booked_on >= DATE '2025-01-01' AND txn.booked_on < DATE '2026-01-01' GROUP BY txn.account_id ORDER BY card_purchases DESC, txn.account_id LIMIT 1

cases.question: What was the net customer flow at each branch in 2025?
cases.intent: Net customer flow is a governed metric — credits minus debits in US dollars on POSTED transactions, internal transfers excluded — not a plain signed sum of every row.
cases.notes: The governed net_customer_flow_usd_minor metric defines it: credits minus debits in amount_usd_minor, POSTED only, TRANSFER_IN/TRANSFER_OUT excluded because an internal transfer only moves money between two accounts inside the bank. Verified against the live fixture 2026-09-28 (seed 20260929, psql): 8 rows (US minor units) — Chicago Loop 47,980,354, Denver LoDo 45,823,688, Atlanta Midtown 34,832,793, Boston Back Bay 29,566,384, Columbus Short North 20,862,294, Charlotte Uptown 19,993,477, Providence College Hill 18,107,317, Hartford Downtown 7,916,372; the reference obeys the dataset's default filter. The two legs of a transfer can sit at different branches, so transfers do not net to zero branch by branch: trapSql keeps them and returns Denver LoDo 48,573,127, Chicago Loop 39,191,218, Atlanta Midtown 37,588,993, Boston Back Bay 31,340,450, Charlotte Uptown 21,193,117, Columbus Short North 19,610,549, Providence College Hill 19,193,843, Hartford Downtown 8,391,382 — every branch differs and the top two swap (differs). Keeping PENDING and REVERSED rows also moves every branch (Chicago Loop 51,495,470). The branch is the ACCOUNT's branch, not the customer's home branch (that path puts Boston Back Bay first at 50,761,824). The figures are checked by the result set; the text check asks for the top branch and the matches check asks the answer to say it left transfers out. In the bare arm (no Metrics) the case is expected to fail or to state its definition. Accepts minor units or dollars — the question names no unit; alternative verified the same day: the same sum / 100.0 returns the same 8 branches, Chicago Loop 479,803.54 down to Hartford Downtown 79,163.72 dollars, each exactly the reference ÷ 100.
cases.expectedSql: SELECT branch.name AS branch, SUM(CASE WHEN txn.direction = 'CREDIT' THEN txn.amount_usd_minor ELSE -txn.amount_usd_minor END) AS net_customer_flow_usd_minor FROM banking.transactions txn JOIN banking.accounts account ON account.id = txn.account_id JOIN banking.branches branch ON branch.id = account.branch_id WHERE account.is_test = false AND txn.status = 'POSTED' AND txn.type NOT IN ('TRANSFER_IN', 'TRANSFER_OUT') AND txn.booked_on >= DATE '2025-01-01' AND txn.booked_on < DATE '2026-01-01' GROUP BY branch.name ORDER BY net_customer_flow_usd_minor DESC, branch.name
expectedSqlAlternatives: SELECT branch.name AS branch, SUM(CASE WHEN txn.direction = 'CREDIT' THEN txn.amount_usd_minor ELSE -txn.amount_usd_minor END) / 100.0 AS net_customer_flow_usd FROM banking.transactions txn JOIN banking.accounts account ON account.id = txn.account_id JOIN banking.branches branch ON branch.id = account.branch_id WHERE account.is_test = false AND txn.status = 'POSTED' AND txn.type NOT IN ('TRANSFER_IN', 'TRANSFER_OUT') AND txn.booked_on >= DATE '2025-01-01' AND txn.booked_on < DATE '2026-01-01' GROUP BY branch.name ORDER BY net_customer_flow_usd DESC, branch.name
cases.trapSql: SELECT branch.name AS branch, SUM(CASE WHEN txn.direction = 'CREDIT' THEN txn.amount_usd_minor ELSE -txn.amount_usd_minor END) AS net_flow_usd_minor FROM banking.transactions txn JOIN banking.accounts account ON account.id = txn.account_id JOIN banking.branches branch ON branch.id = account.branch_id WHERE account.is_test = false AND txn.status = 'POSTED' AND txn.booked_on >= DATE '2025-01-01' AND txn.booked_on < DATE '2026-01-01' GROUP BY branch.name

cases.question: How many transactions did we record in March 2025?
variants: What was our transaction count for March 2025?
How many transactions were booked in March 2025?
cases.intent: Sandbox test accounts are flagged and their traffic must come out of a reported volume without being asked for.
cases.notes: 6 of the 200 accounts are is_test = true sandbox accounts (3.0%), and the Banking dataset carries a default-filter knowledge entry saying to exclude them, their cards and their transactions. Their traffic is concentrated in March 2025: 14 of their 36 transactions. Verified against the live fixture 2026-09-28 (seed 20260929, psql): 1 row — 236 transactions booked in March 2025 on real accounts; 250 with the test traffic. The count covers every status (a reversed transaction was still recorded; POSTED only would be 222). Every transactions reference in this suite obeys the default filter; this is the case that makes it the question, so its wording never pre-announces it. The count is checked by the result set; the matches check asks the answer to say it left test traffic out. trapSql drops the default filter and returns 250 (differs). Guards against test traffic leaking into reported volumes.
cases.expectedSql: SELECT COUNT(*) AS transactions FROM banking.transactions txn JOIN banking.accounts account ON account.id = txn.account_id WHERE account.is_test = false AND txn.booked_on >= DATE '2025-03-01' AND txn.booked_on < DATE '2025-04-01'
cases.trapSql: SELECT COUNT(*) AS transactions FROM banking.transactions txn WHERE txn.booked_on >= DATE '2025-03-01' AND txn.booked_on < DATE '2025-04-01'

cases.question: How many accounts were opened in each region in 2024?
cases.intent: Accounts carry a branch, not a region — the answer needs accounts -> branches -> regions, and not the customer's home branch.
cases.notes: The path is accounts.branch_id -> branches.region_id -> regions.name. customers.home_branch_id is a lookalike path: 38 of the 200 accounts sit at a branch other than the owner's home branch. Verified against the live fixture 2026-09-28 (seed 20260929, psql): 4 rows — Southeast 20, Midwest 18, Northeast 13, West 6 (57 real accounts opened in 2024; 59 with the test accounts). trapSql goes through the customer's home branch instead and returns Southeast 20, Midwest 17, Northeast 16, West 4 (differs in three of the four regions). Stopping one join short reports 8 branches at the wrong grain. The counts are checked by the result set; the text check asks for the largest region by name. Guards against the plausible-but-wrong join path and against answers that stop short of the requested grain.
cases.expectedSql: SELECT region.name AS region, COUNT(*) AS accounts_opened FROM banking.accounts account JOIN banking.branches branch ON branch.id = account.branch_id JOIN banking.regions region ON region.id = branch.region_id WHERE account.is_test = false AND account.opened_on >= DATE '2024-01-01' AND account.opened_on < DATE '2025-01-01' GROUP BY region.name ORDER BY accounts_opened DESC, region.name
cases.trapSql: SELECT region.name AS region, COUNT(*) AS accounts_opened FROM banking.accounts account JOIN banking.customers customer ON customer.id = account.customer_id JOIN banking.branches branch ON branch.id = customer.home_branch_id JOIN banking.regions region ON region.id = branch.region_id WHERE account.is_test = false AND account.opened_on >= DATE '2024-01-01' AND account.opened_on < DATE '2025-01-01' GROUP BY region.name

cases.question: How many deposit accounts have been opened at each branch?
variants: For each branch, how many deposit accounts has it opened?
cases.intent: "Deposit account" is a product category (checking, savings, money market) — credit cards and lines of credit are accounts too, but not deposit accounts.
cases.notes: account_types.category splits the five products into DEPOSIT (Everyday Checking, High-Yield Savings, Money Market Account) and CREDIT (Rewards Credit Card, Personal Line of Credit); "deposit accounts" is that category, not the DEPOSIT transaction type. Verified against the live fixture 2026-09-28 (seed 20260929, psql): 8 rows — Chicago Loop 34, Atlanta Midtown 22, Columbus Short North 17, Boston Back Bay 15, Charlotte Uptown 14, Denver LoDo 14, Providence College Hill 13, Hartford Downtown 9 (real accounts of every status, closed ones included — "have been opened"). trapSql counts every account regardless of category and returns Chicago Loop 42, Charlotte Uptown 29, Atlanta Midtown 27, Boston Back Bay 26, Denver LoDo 23, Columbus Short North 19, Providence College Hill 17, Hartford Downtown 11 (differs at every branch — the generator asserts each branch holds at least one real credit account). The counts are checked by the result set; the text check asks for the largest branch. Guards against treating every account as a deposit account.
cases.expectedSql: SELECT branch.name AS branch, COUNT(*) AS deposit_accounts FROM banking.accounts account JOIN banking.account_types account_type ON account_type.id = account.account_type_id JOIN banking.branches branch ON branch.id = account.branch_id WHERE account.is_test = false AND account_type.category = 'DEPOSIT' GROUP BY branch.name ORDER BY deposit_accounts DESC, branch.name
cases.trapSql: SELECT branch.name AS branch, COUNT(*) AS accounts FROM banking.accounts account JOIN banking.branches branch ON branch.id = account.branch_id WHERE account.is_test = false GROUP BY branch.name

cases.question: How much did customers deposit in 2025, in US dollars?
variants: In US dollars, what was the total value of customer deposits in 2025?
cases.intent: amount_minor is in each account's own currency — a US-dollar total needs amount_usd_minor, divided by 100.
cases.notes: EUR and GBP accounts store amount_minor in euro cents and pence; amount_usd_minor is the booking month's conversion at the fx_rates rate (equal to amount_minor on USD accounts). Verified against the live fixture 2026-09-28 (seed 20260929, psql): 1 row — 2,596,749.29 US dollars from 682 POSTED 2025 deposits on real accounts (605 on USD accounts, 53 EUR, 24 GBP). trapSql adds amount_minor across currencies and returns 2,555,993.20 (differs — euro cents and pence summed as if they were US cents). Reporting the minor-unit sum as dollars would be 100x off (259,674,929). Keeping PENDING and REVERSED deposits gives 2,774,543.52; adding internal TRANSFER_IN gives 2,844,918.33 — neither is money customers deposited. The figure is checked by the result set. Guards against mixing currencies and minor units in a money answer.
cases.expectedSql: SELECT ROUND(SUM(txn.amount_usd_minor) / 100.0, 2) AS deposits_usd FROM banking.transactions txn JOIN banking.accounts account ON account.id = txn.account_id WHERE account.is_test = false AND txn.type = 'DEPOSIT' AND txn.status = 'POSTED' AND txn.booked_on >= DATE '2025-01-01' AND txn.booked_on < DATE '2026-01-01'
cases.trapSql: SELECT ROUND(SUM(txn.amount_minor) / 100.0, 2) AS deposits FROM banking.transactions txn JOIN banking.accounts account ON account.id = txn.account_id WHERE account.is_test = false AND txn.type = 'DEPOSIT' AND txn.status = 'POSTED' AND txn.booked_on >= DATE '2025-01-01' AND txn.booked_on < DATE '2026-01-01'

cases.question: How much was deposited into our euro-denominated accounts in 2025, in euros?
variants: In euros, what was the total deposited into our euro accounts during 2025?
cases.intent: The mirror of the US-dollar case: asked in euros, the account-currency amount_minor is right and the converted amount_usd_minor is wrong.
cases.notes: Verified against the live fixture 2026-09-28 (seed 20260929, psql): 1 row — 340,142.08 euros from 53 POSTED 2025 deposits into the 14 EUR accounts (none of them test accounts). trapSql reports the US-dollar conversion and returns 370,332.90 (differs). Here amount_minor — the account-currency amount — is the right column, the opposite of customer-deposits-2025-usd, so a fix that always reaches for amount_usd_minor fails this case. Keeping PENDING and REVERSED deposits gives 359,039.38. The figure is checked by the result set. Guards against a currency conversion applied where none was asked for.

cases.question: What information do we hold about cards?
cases.intent: Pure discovery — must answer from the session datasets rather than run SQL or invent entities.
cases.notes: A schema question answered by querying rows is a wrong process even when the prose happens to be right, so this case scores the process and the entity names. Verified against the live fixture 2026-09-28 (seed 20260929, psql): cards holds 150 rows — card_number_masked, network (VISA/MASTERCARD), card_type (DEBIT 100, all on checking accounts; CREDIT 50, all on credit-card accounts), issued_on, expires_on, status (ACTIVE/BLOCKED/EXPIRED/CANCELLED) and account_id; card purchases are transactions of type CARD_PURCHASE carrying card_id and merchant_category. No PIN, CVV, credit limit, rewards or full card number exists anywhere in the schema. The entity list is already in the per-turn system block, so no list_entities check. Guards against the engine reaching for run_readonly_sql on questions about what exists.
cases.judgeRubric: The user asks what data exists about cards; the correct answer names the relevant entities without running SQL. It names cards (one row per issued card: a masked card number, the network VISA or MASTERCARD, the card type DEBIT or CREDIT, issued_on and expires_on dates, a status of ACTIVE, BLOCKED, EXPIRED or CANCELLED, and the account it belongs to — debit cards on checking accounts, credit cards on credit-card accounts) and the accounts it links to, and may add that card purchases are recorded in transactions (type CARD_PURCHASE, with the card and a merchant category). Score pass=true only if the final answer names both cards and accounts (by name or an unambiguous equivalent), says what cards holds, and no run_readonly_sql call was made. Score pass=false if it ran SQL against the data, invents a card attribute the dataset does not have (e.g. a PIN, CVV, credit limit, rewards points, cardholder name or full card number), or names only the transactions table. Close but wrong: an answer that only describes card purchases in transactions and never mentions the cards table, or that names cards but invents a column such as a credit limit or a spending cap — that must FAIL.

cases.question: How many customers do we have in each segment?
variants: What's our customer count by segment?
Break down our customers by segment.
cases.intent: One table, one GROUP BY, no trap — the healthy baseline for this fixture.
cases.notes: Verified against the live fixture 2026-09-28 (seed 20260929, psql): 3 rows — RETAIL 55, PREMIER 19, BUSINESS 16, totalling all 90 customers. No ratio, no nulls, no money, no accounts and therefore no default filter to apply (customers carry no test flag): if this fails, the problem is schema linking rather than any planted trap, and no guard may fire on it. The counts are checked by the result set. The reference is portable SQL, so it needs no Databricks override.
cases.expectedSql: SELECT customer.segment, COUNT(*) AS customers FROM banking.customers customer GROUP BY customer.segment ORDER BY customers DESC, customer.segment

cases.question: How many branches do we have in each region?
cases.intent: A single join and GROUP BY over reference data, no filter implied by the question.
cases.notes: Verified against the live fixture 2026-09-28 (seed 20260929, psql): 4 rows — Northeast 3, Midwest 2, Southeast 2, West 1, totalling all 8 branches. regions.code holds the upper-case form (MIDWEST) and regions.name the display form (Midwest); the result-set check and the includes check both compare case-insensitively, so either column passes. The counterpart to accounts-opened-by-region-2024: this one counts BRANCHES, so a fix that reflexively joins to accounts or customers over-fires here. The reference is portable SQL, so it needs no Databricks override. Guards against guards firing on an ordinary question.
cases.expectedSql: SELECT region.name AS region, COUNT(*) AS branches FROM banking.branches branch JOIN banking.regions region ON region.id = branch.region_id GROUP BY region.name ORDER BY branches DESC, region.name
